title: Multiplicative Noise in Nanolaser Amplification: From Discrete Emission Events to the Additive-Noise Limit
authors: G. Sonnino, Ph. Peeters, P. Nardone, G. L. Lippi
abstract: Laser amplification kicks off with just a few photons in the cavity, a regime where standard additive Langevin noise cannot capture the real fluctuations. To understand how this amplification begins, we map out a single-mode photon-carrier model that links macroscopic lasers directly into nanolasers. Stationary rate equations reveal that stimulated emission takes over across a tight pump window. In nanolasers, however, spontaneous processes coexist across a much broader range. Because steady-state averages miss the individual events that lead to the macroscopic photon number, we frame the stochastic dynamics around the actual discrete transitions, deriving a state-dependent diffusion approximation. The destruction of an excited carrier concurrent with the generation of a photon creates a negative photon-carrier cross-correlation. This unavoidably leads to a correlated, multiplicative Gaussian-noise framework. We track the resulting discrete dynamics with an established, event-based Laser Markov Chain (LMC) which stochastically samples pump, relaxation, emission, and cavity-loss events keeping all physical quantities as non-negative integers. Comparing its predictions to those of our multiplicative model proves that the latter reproduces excellently well the statistical behavior of photons and carrier, as long as a continuous diffusion description holds. Once the emission drops into the few-photon regime, however, the discrete model becomes indispensable. On the other hand, at large photon counts relative fluctuations shrink to a level where the state-dependence of the diffusion matrix can be ignored, to leading order, thus returning to the classic Langevin description of the system's stochastic dynamics.
summary: This paper develops a comprehensive stochastic model for laser amplification, recognizing that standard additive noise models fail when the photon count is low. By deriving a multiplicative noise framework from discrete event simulations, the authors show that this model accurately captures the physics near threshold. It demonstrates a clear physical crossover: discrete events dominate at low counts, while the system smoothly approaches the well-known additive Langevin description at high counts.
main_problem: The paper addresses the failure of standard additive noise models to accurately describe the initial, few-photon stages of laser amplification, where discrete emission events dominate.
main_result: A multiplicative Gaussian noise framework, derived from an event-based Laser Markov Chain, accurately reproduces the statistical behavior in the low-photon regime, while correctly recovering the classic additive Langevin description at high photon counts.
method: The authors employ a comparison between an event-based simulation (Laser Markov Chain) and a derived state-dependent diffusion approximation (multiplicative noise model).
model_or_system: The system is a nanolaser undergoing amplification, modeled using a single-mode photon-carrier framework. The dynamics transition from discrete, event-driven processes to continuous diffusion processes.
key_observables: Photon number, carrier population, and the statistical distribution of these quantities.
important_parameters: The ratio of gain to loss ($r$), the operating regime (few-photon vs. high-photon), and the spontaneous emission factor ($ eta$).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the system dynamics can be accurately mapped across three regimes: discrete (LMC), continuous multiplicative (diffusion), and classical additive (Langevin).
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the probability of initiating lasing as a function of the gain-to-loss ratio ($r$), confirming the conceptual threshold at $r=1$.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first noting the failure of simple rate equations, deriving a correlated, multiplicative Gaussian noise model from discrete transitions, and finally validating this model against the rigorous, event-based Laser Markov Chain, showing the recovery of the additive limit at high counts.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to open quantum systems and quantum optics as it provides a rigorous mathematical framework for modeling noise evolution across different physical regimes, bridging the gap between discrete quantum jumps and continuous classical noise approximations.
